- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.33) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — consider slight upward correction.  
- When true outcome shows sharp spikes or drops after a flat period, model often lags — adjust forecast to anticipate early reversal.  
- If forecast is trending upward but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20%.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67) and forecast is flat, consider slight upward bias — market may react to sentiment shifts.  
- Avoid forecasting linear trends when sentiment shows strong volatility — use smoothing or adaptive decay for short-term corrections.  
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome by 3–5% over 30d, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to align with mean reversion.  
- If sentiment turns negative after a spike, forecast should not continue rising — apply early correction to prevent overshoot.
